content.title: About
content.content: Country fried beef steak is a cut of meat, usually from the sirloin or ribeye, breaded in a seasoned flour mixture and pan‑fried until golden and crispy. The result is a tender steak with a crunchy coating, often served with potatoes and vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “country fried” comes from Southern U.S. cooking, where the dish was traditionally prepared on a farm over an open fire.
Typical breading includes paprika, garlic powder, and dried herbs such as rosemary and thyme.
Beef provides heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.
In the United States the dish is often served with barbecue sauce or a mustard‑based gravy.
A classic “country fried steak” may be lightly pounded before breading to ensure even cooking.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef steak supplies complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Heme iron from beef supports healthy hemoglobin levels and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Steak is a good source of B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals aid immune function and act as antioxidants.

items.title: Creatine
items.content: Natural creatine in beef can improve physical performance and muscle endurance.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Excessive intake may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Added sodium in breading
items.content: Prepared versions often contain extra salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked beef can harbor harmful bacteria such as E. coli.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional breading uses wheat flour, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the country fried steak hot, typically alongside mashed potatoes, fries, or a vegetable medley. It pairs well with barbecue sauce, mushroom gravy, or a simple butter sauce. For a lighter version, use whole‑grain flour or a gluten‑free coating.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw beef refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in a sealed bag for 2‑3 days. Cooked steak should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days or frozen for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Coffee cake is a moist, crumbly quick‑bread style cake made with ground coffee and fruit (such as berries, apples or cherries). It combines the aromatic flavor of coffee with the natural sweetness of fruit, resulting in a tender crumb and a soft texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Coffee cake is often served at breakfast or as an afternoon snack, especially in Northern European countries.
Adding fruit increases the cake’s moisture and reduces the need for large amounts of sugar.
Coffee enhances aroma without making the cake overly bitter when a moderate amount of ground coffee or espresso is used.
Traditional recipes rely on baking powder, so the cake rises quickly without yeast.
The batter can be baked in a muffin tin, creating convenient single‑serve portions.

items.title: Caffeine boost
items.content: Caffeine in coffee stimulates the central nervous system, improving alertness and concentration.

items.title: Fruit antioxidants
items.content: Berries and other fruits added to the cake are rich in vitamin C and polyphenols, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fruit and whole‑grain flour (if used) provide fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Coffee contributes magnesium and potassium, while fruit adds iron and folate, important for metabolic processes.

items.title: Reduced added sugar
items.content: Natural fruit sweetness allows the recipe to use less added sugar, making the cake less calorie‑dense.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: People sensitive to caffeine should limit portion size to avoid nervousness or sleep disturbances.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: The cake may contain nuts, dairy, or gluten, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Despite fruit sweetness, the cake still contains added sugar; individuals with diabetes should monitor portions.

items.title: Fruit acidity
items.content: Acidic fruits can increase batter acidity, sometimes leading to faster browning of the crust.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the coffee cake at room temperature, often alongside a cup of coffee or tea. Slice it into wedges, top with cream cheese or yogurt, and enjoy as a snack or light dessert. The cake keeps well in the refrigerator for daily snacking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cake in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days or in the refrigerator for up to a week. For longer storage, freeze it in a freezer‑safe bag – it retains flavor and texture for 2‑3 months. Thaw at room temperature before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: A doughnut is a small sweet fried or baked pastry made from dough, often glazed or topped with sprinkles. The plain version without filling is a round bun with a hole in the middle, made from yeasted dough and fried in oil until golden.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Doughnuts appeared in Europe in the 17th century and quickly became a staple for the working class.
The classic American "donut" is ring‑shaped, but in Russia simple hole‑less doughnuts are also popular.
In Japan there are "caramel doughnuts" coated with a rich caramel glaze.
Doughnuts are commonly served with coffee as a quick snack.
There are countless glaze varieties: sugar, chocolate, fruit, and more.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Doughnuts provide fast‑acting carbohydrates that quickly replenish energy stores.

items.title: B‑vitamin content
items.content: Yeasted dough contains B1, B2, and B6 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Flour and yeast contribute a modest amount of iron, beneficial for blood health.

items.title: High sugar and fat
items.content: Excessive consumption can lead to weight gain and elevated blood sugar levels.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional doughnuts are made with wheat flour, making them unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Trans fats from frying
items.content: Frying in oil can create trans fats, which are harmful to cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Doughnuts are usually enjoyed warm, dusted with powdered sugar, glazed, or filled with jam, cream, or chocolate. They are convenient as a quick on‑the‑go snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store doughnuts in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze them and reheat in the oven before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Raw fish is a seafood product obtained directly after catch and without any heat treatment. It is rich in high‑quality protein, omega‑3 fatty acids, vitamins D and B12, as well as minerals such as selenium and iodine. Raw fish is enjoyed as sashimi, carpaccio, marinated dishes, and as part of sushi.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Raw fish is a staple in Japanese, Korean and Scandinavian cuisines.
Omega‑3 fatty acids EPA and DHA found in fish support heart and brain health.
Certain species, like farmed salmon, are raised in controlled aquaculture environments to limit contaminants.
Raw fish must be stored at temperatures between 0 °C and +4 °C to prevent bacterial growth.
Traditional serving involves thin slices accompanied by soy sauce, wasabi and pickled ginger.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Raw fish provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: EPA and DHA help maintain cardiovascular health, reduce inflammation, and support brain development.

items.title: Vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D from fish enhances calcium absorption and promotes bone health.

items.title: Iodine and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals are crucial for thyroid function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with many meat products, raw fish contains mainly polyunsaturated fats.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Raw fish may harbor parasites (Anisakis, Opisthorchis) and bacteria (Salmonella, Listeria). Purchase from reputable sources and keep properly refrigerated.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals can experience severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: Large predatory species (tiger, swordfish) can accumulate mercury; intake should be limited, especially for pregnant women and children.

items.title: Not suitable for young children
items.content: The firm texture and possible parasites make raw fish unsafe for children under 5 years old.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice raw fish thinly and serve with soy sauce, wasabi, ginger, lemon or vinegar. It is also used in rolls, sashimi, carpaccio and marinades. Keep the fish chilled and serve immediately after slicing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw fish in an airtight container at 0 °C to +4 °C for no more than 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C and thaw in the refrigerator before use. Discard fish with off‑odors, discolored flesh or a slimy surface.

content.title: About
content.content: Tuna is a marine fish from the mackerel family, widely used in cuisine. The NFS (Not From Salmon) variant refers to tuna caught in the open ocean without salmon contamination. Tuna has firm flesh, a mild flavor, and a high protein content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tuna can swim at speeds up to 70 km/h.
The largest species, the bluefin tuna, can weigh over 600 kg.
Tuna is a staple for sushi and sashimi because of its texture and taste.
Its meat is rich in omega‑3 fatty acids, beneficial for heart health.
In some cultures tuna is considered a delicacy and served as grilled steaks.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Tuna provides about 23 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of omega‑3
items.content: EPA and DHA omega‑3s help maintain cardiovascular health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many meats, tuna is low in calories and saturated fat.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Rich in B12, niacin, and B6, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Contains selenium, iodine, and magnesium, important for thyroid function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: Large tuna can accumulate mercury; pregnant women and children should limit intake.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including tuna.

items.title: Sodium in canned form
items.content: Canned tuna often contains added salt, which may be a concern for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tuna can be served as steaks, baked, grilled, or used in salads and sandwiches. Sushi chefs often serve it raw as sashimi. Canned tuna is convenient for quick meals.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh tuna should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C for no more than 2 days. Frozen tuna lasts up to 6 months at –18 °C. Canned tuna can be stored in a dry place until the expiration date.

content.title: About
content.content: Pad Thai with seafood is a classic Thai dish made from rice noodles stir‑fried with egg, tofu, shrimp, squid, bean sprouts, green onions and peanuts, flavored with a sauce of tamarind, fish sauce, lime and palm sugar.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish was created in the 1930s as part of Thailand’s national culinary campaign.
Tamarind gives the sauce its distinctive sweet‑sour taste.
Traditionally it is served with a lime wedge and crushed peanuts, though the seafood version often uses cashews.
Pad Thai is a fast street‑food staple: it can be cooked in 5‑10 minutes over high heat.
Original recipes use medium‑width rice noodles, but regional variations may use thinner or wider strands.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Shrimp and squid provide high‑quality marine protein that supports tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of omega‑3
items.content: Seafood contributes beneficial omega‑3 fatty acids, which promote heart and brain health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tamarind and soy sauce are good sources of vitamin B6 and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Lime and cashews supply vitamin C and vitamin E, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Fiber
items.content: Bean sprouts and whole‑grain rice noodles add dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Shrimp and squid can trigger severe allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Fish sauce and soy sauce are salty; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional soy sauce may contain gluten; choose a gluten‑free version for celiac disease.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Improperly cooked seafood can harbor bacteria and parasites.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve Pad Thai hot, straight from the wok. Squeeze fresh lime juice over it, toss with crushed cashews, and add sliced chili if desired. It can be eaten with chopsticks or a fork.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in a pan or microwave, adding a splash of water to keep the noodles from drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Butter flavored ready‑to‑eat popcorn is made from air‑popped corn kernels that are lightly toasted and coated with a savory butter seasoning. It requires no preparation, stays fresh for months, and is ideal for a quick snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popcorn is one of the oldest snacks, enjoyed by ancient Mesoamerican cultures.
Each kernel contains a small amount of moisture; when heated, the moisture turns to steam and makes the kernel explode.
The butter flavor is achieved with a blend of vegetable oils and natural flavorings, without real dairy butter.
Popcorn is highly portable and retains its crunch and taste over long periods.
In the United States popcorn is synonymous with movie theaters, while in Russia it has become a popular home snack.

items.title: Relatively low in calories
items.content: Popcorn provides about 380 kcal per 100 g, which is lower than most chips and crackers.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Polysaccharides and polyphenols in popcorn help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Naturally free of gluten, making it suitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Popcorn provides thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Salt and fat content
items.content: Some butter‑flavored versions can be high in sodium and added oils; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Although rare, corn allergy can cause skin or respiratory reactions.

items.title: Choking hazard for young children
items.content: Small pieces may pose a choking risk for toddlers; supervision is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Popcorn is ready to eat straight from the bag. It can be enjoyed as a snack, tossed into salads, used as a topping for soups or desserts, or seasoned further with paprika, garlic powder, or cheese flavorings.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep popcorn in a sealed package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For extended shelf life store it in the refrigerator to preserve crunch and flavor. Discard if it becomes moist, loses aroma, or develops a rancid smell.
